2.  Dakota 
 
Program Name:  Dakota.java 
Input File:  dakota.dat 
 
Dakota’s mom owns a parts warehouse.  Dakota has been asked to help out by writing a program to read in a customer name and 
items from an order and then produce an invoice to provide to their customers.  Their invoice should include calculations for 
subtotals and Texas Sales Tax at the rate of 8.25%. 
 
Input:   
The first line of the data file contains a single integer representing the number of orders to be processed. 
For each order, the first line contains the customer name (as a single word).  The next line contains an integer representing the 
number of different items having been ordered.  Each of the next lines contain an item name (single word), quantity (an integer), 
and a unit price (a real number). 
 
Output:   
The invoice will contain section breaks which will consist of a single plus (+), 42 dashes (-), and end with a single plus (+).  
One of these such lines will also be the first and last line of each invoice. The first and last character of each of the remaining 
lines will be the “or” or “pipe” character (|), found above the return/enter key on your keyboard.  There will be a single space 
as a “buffer” between the outer lines and the information inside.  The title for the invoice is. “Invoice for C” where C is the 
customer name.  In the next section, you will print the column titles spread out as follows: Item, followed by 9 spaces, Qty, 5 
spaces, Price, 5 spaces, Subtotal.  The next section will have each item starting under the I in Item above, the quantity right 
justified ending under the t of Qty above, the unit price with the decimals aligned under the i in Price above, and the item total 
with the decimals aligned under to o in Subtotal above.  In the last section, we will have 3 lines:  Subtotal, Tax, and Total. 
Each of those start with a one-space “buffer” before the words and each needs to be followed immediately by a :.  Each of the 
values for these lines are aligned by the decimal which is aligned under the a in Subtotal in the title section up above.  There will 
be no blank lines in between invoices—immediately start the next invoice.

2 
BOB 
1 
Motor 3 38.79 
RUMI 
3 
Servo 4 12.50 
Wheel 2 18.75 
Battery 1 49.99

+------------------------------------------+

+------------------------------------------+

| Total:                            125.97 |

| Tax:                               11.34 | 
| Total:                            148.83 |

3.  Logan 
 
Program Name:  Logan.java 
Input File:  logan.dat 
 
Logan’s meat judging team is having a Cow Patty Bingo fundraiser.  No one from the team wants to go around and actually 
locate the patties on the football field because no one wants to accidentally step on one.  Logan attached a sensor to his drone 
that takes atmospheric readings and can “detect” the patties to a certain degree of certainty.  The data is presented in a grid.  
Logan needs to display a “hazard map” and the list of one-based coordinate location(s) with the highest reading. 
 
Input:   
The first line contains an integer representing the number of test cases.  For each test case the first line will contain 3 integers:  
R, C, and T representing the number of rows and columns in the grid and the threshold reading that indicates the likelihood of a 
cow patty being present in that grid location.  This is followed by R rows, each with C readings. 
 
Output:   
Title each output case “--- Hazard Map Case X ---” where X is the test case number.  Display the original grid with 
each reading right justified in a “cell” of 3 spaces with “Grid:” as a label at the beginning.  Then a blank line.  Then a line 
“Smelliest value: X” where X is the highest reading in the grid.  Next a line “Location(s) :” followed by a list of 
all the 1-based coordinates where the highest reading happened.  If there are more than one, simply separate them with a single 
space.  This needs to be followed with a blank line.  Finally, title the hazard grid “Hazard map:” and display the grid with . 
for “safe” zones and X for hazardous zones.  These should be separated by a single space. Add a blank line to the end of each 
test case output. 
 
Sample input: 
1 
3 5 70 
55 70 61 88 40 
72 68 70 59 90 
33 71 45 70 70 
 
Sample output: 
--- Hazard Map Case 1 --- 
Grid: 
 55 70 61 88 40 
 72 68 70 59 90 
 33 71 45 70 70 
 
Smelliest value: 90 
Location(s)  : (2,5) 
 
Danger map: 
. X . X . 
X . X . X 
. X . X X

Your buddy Austin is a bit of a nuisance in class, and has been trying to pass you notes, but does not want the teacher to see

4 
3 [ good at mathema] 
1 [This Teacher i] 
4 [tics. LOL HAHAHA] 
2 [s not very] 
 
Sample output:  
This Teacher is not very good at mathematics. LOL HAHAHA

5.  Bingo 
 
Program Name:  Bingo.java 
Input File:  bingo.dat 
 
While visiting your family for the holidays you decided to play bingo. While at the bingo hall your grandmother seemed to keep 
winning repeatedly. Of course, she credits it to her amazing bingo skill, but you suspect that her bingo card might be better than 
yours. To test this theory, you made note of your grandmother’s bingo card and decided to simulate some games against other 
random bingo cards to see the results. 
 
Input:   
The first 5 lines of input will each contain 5 space separated numbers, each denoting a bingo slot on your grandmother’s bingo 
card. The following line will contain a single integer N (1 <= N <= 100) denoting the number of test cases. Each game will start 
with a single integer C (1 <= C <= 10) denoting the number of bingo cards in this game (not including your grandmother’s card) 
and a random seed to be used for the game. There will then be 5C following lines each with 5 space separated numbers, each 5 
lines being a 5x5 bingo card. 
 
To simulate a game, use the random seed provided and generate a value between 1 and 75 (inclusive) and mark the appropriate 
spaces on each bingo card. Once one or more players have filled a row, column, or diagonal they will win that game. 
 
Note that the middle square of every card will contain 0, denoting a free space (already marked). 
 
Output:   
For each test case, simulate 1000 bingo games. Then, output what percentage of games your grandmother won in the format

Julia wants to get back at her sister with a better puzzle, as she got stumped by the palindrome “insertion” problem. She has 
decided to request your help in checking her work. She wants to see if, given a directed graph, are there any cycles in the graph, 
she does not think Liz knows anything about graphs. You will be given the number of nodes, and all the connections within the 
graph. A cycle is defined as a path in a graph that starts and ends at the same vertex, with no edges or other vertices repeated, 
forming a closed loop. 
 
Input:

number of nodes in the graph, and the number of connections you will be given, respectively. The following c lines will each 
contain a pair of 0-indexed integers (a b) denoting a connection from node index a to node index b, and do NOT indicate a 
connection from b to a exists as well. 
 
Output:   
For each test case, if there is a cycle in the graph, output the string “Lizn't that interesting.”, otherwise output 
“Juliain't gonna beat me.”.

3 
4 4 
0 1 
1 2

3 2

Program Name:  Sciel.java 
Input File:  sciel.dat 
 
Sciel is good friends with Sophie who recently got her addicted to a game called “Ticket to Ride”. In this game, each 
player obtains different train cards, which they can spend to complete their routes assigned to them. The board can 
effectively be abstracted out to a set of vertices (cities) and edges (a series of trains owned by at most a single 
player). A player is only allowed to place their trains along an edge between two cities so long as (1) there is an 
unclaimed edge between the two cities, and (2) they possess enough colored train cards corresponding to the number 
of colored slots for the unclaimed route. For non-adjacent cities, a player is said to connect them together if and only 
if there exists some set of contiguous edges between the two cities that the player owns. Given Sciel’s hand of 
colored train cards, the board, and a route consisting of a starting and ending city, help Sciel determine if she can 
complete her route by connecting the two cities together. 
 
Input:   
The first line will consist of a single integer 𝑇, 1 ≤𝑇≤50, denoting the number of testcases to follow. Each of the 
following 𝑇 lines will consist of the serialized object string corresponding to the board, hand, and route that Sciel 
wishes to investigate. For each test case, you may assume that there are less than 100 cities, less than 500 edges, at 
most 15 of each colored card in Sciel’s hand, and colors consist of either Red, Green, Blue, Yellow, or Pink. You 
may also assume that each graph representation of the board will be undirected. 
 
Output:   
For each test case, on its own line, if it is possible to complete the route, then output the string  
“Tomorrow comes”, otherwise, instead print “When one falls, we continue”

2

Tomorrow comes 
When one falls, we continue

The first testcase consists of three cities (Berlin, London, and Paris), with an edge between Berlin and London 
costing three blue cards and an edge between London and Paris costing two red cards. Your hand consists of exactly
